Antonio López de Santa Anna. The Mexican military general and politician who served as president at least eleven times between 1833 and 1855, embodying the country's political instability in the nineteenth century.

Santa Anna alternated between liberal and conservative factions, becoming the nation's most powerful figure during the early republic. His military record, however, was marked by dramatic defeats that cost Mexico vast territories. In 1836, he defeated Texan rebels at the Alamo, but he was himself captured after his loss at San Jacinto, and this led directly to Texan independence. Two decades later, he led Mexican forces in the Mexican-American War from 1846 to 1848, suffering defeats that forced Mexico to cede the Southwest and California. He signed the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, which meant Mexico lost nearly half of its total territory—the greatest territorial loss in the nation's history. Despite these military failures, he returned to power repeatedly, embodying both the ambitions and the weaknesses of post-independence Mexico. He died in obscurity in Mexico City in 1876, a symbol of an era's military and political chaos. Benito Juárez, the reformer who came after him, would chart a very different course for Mexico's future.
